Devdiscourse News Desk | Geneva | Updated: 09-11-2026 12:59 IST | Created: 09-11-2026 12:59 IST Scientists are investigating possible treatments for people who have contracted Bundibugyo virus disease through the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS clinical trial, launched in July 2026. Image Credit: ChatGPT SHARE Key Takeaways AI Summary Analyzing article... Two experimental Ebola vaccines designed to protect against Bundibugyo virus could soon be tested during an active outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), following recommendations from expert groups convened by the World Health Organization (WHO). The vaccines are expected to join the ongoing Tumaini clinical trial once national authorities approve their inclusion, creating the first opportunity to evaluate vaccines specifically developed for Bundibugyo virus during an outbreak. Researchers hope the findings will help identify new ways to protect communities exposed to the virus and strengthen future responses to similar health emergencies. The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469, which uses messenger RNA technology. WHO's independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization recommended both vaccines for further clinical evaluation after reviewing available laboratory research and early clinical evidence. Their inclusion in the trial represents an important development in efforts to understand whether these vaccines can provide effective protection against Bundibugyo virus disease. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus described the progress as an example of what scientific cooperation can achieve, recognising the contributions of researchers, healthcare workers, international partners and people participating in the trial. He emphasised that vaccines alone cannot end the outbreak, but successful candidates could provide health authorities with another valuable tool to reduce infections and protect vulnerable communities. The participation of people exposed to the virus will help researchers gather evidence needed to understand vaccine effectiveness and guide future public health decisions. New Vaccines Bring Hope for Stronger Ebola Protection The Tumaini vaccine trial is being led by the DRC's Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB), working closely with Belgium's University of Antwerp and several international health organisations. Partners include WHO, Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières, the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the DRC Ministry of Health and the country's Institut National de Santé Publique. Investments from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) have supported the rapid development of vaccine candidates, helping researchers prepare potential protective tools for outbreaks involving different Ebola viruses. The trial allows researchers to evaluate multiple vaccine candidates within a single research programme, making it possible to gather evidence about different approaches to preventing Bundibugyo virus disease. Oxford's ChAdOx1 and Moderna's mRNA-1469 will enter the programme only after the necessary national approvals have been granted, and the required clinical arrangements are completed. Studying these vaccines during an outbreak could provide valuable information about their performance in real-world conditions, including whether they can reduce the risk of illness among people exposed to infected individuals. How Ring Vaccination Could Help Control the Outbreak The Tumaini trial follows a ring-vaccination approach, which involves identifying people who have been in contact with someone diagnosed with Bundibugyo virus disease and enrolling eligible contacts in the research. Four vaccination rings have been established, with additional groups being prepared to include contacts of people who became ill or died from Ebola. This approach allows researchers to study vaccine effectiveness among people with known exposure risks and could provide useful evidence for improving outbreak responses. The strategy draws on experience from the Ebola outbreak in West Africa about a decade ago, when WHO and its partners conducted a major vaccine trial in Guinea. That research demonstrated the effectiveness of Ervebo against Ebola virus, commonly known as Zaire ebolavirus, and helped establish ring vaccination as an important research approach during outbreaks. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in the current Tumaini trial to determine whether it offers protection against Bundibugyo virus, with the two newly recommended candidates expected to expand the research once approved. New Treatment Research Could Improve Patient Survival Scientists are investigating possible treatments for people who have contracted Bundibugyo virus disease through the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS clinical trial, launched in July 2026. The research is examining whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral medicine remdesivir or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed infections. Another treatment called maftivimab is expected to enter the trial, and a separate study is evaluating obeldevisir as a possible preventive medicine after exposure to the virus. WHO is supporting these studies through its Research and Development Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme, helping researchers develop protocols, coordinate partnerships and conduct scientifically rigorous and ethical research during the outbreak. Initial findings from the treatment trials are expected in the coming months, with results from the Tumaini vaccine trial anticipated in early 2027. The move marks an important step in efforts to develop vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus, which is responsible for the current Ebola outbreak. The recommendation also marks the first time that vaccines specifically developed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus will undergo evaluation during an active outbreak. Two New Vaccine Candidates Recommended The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469. WHO’s independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization recommended both candidates for further clinical evaluation based on available preclinical and early clinical evidence. The candidates will join the ongoing Tumaini trial once they receive the necessary national approvals. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus highlighted the importance of scientific collaboration and clinical research in tackling the outbreak. He noted that the participation of researchers, healthcare workers and trial volunteers would help generate vital evidence to support future outbreak responses. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) has also supported the rapid development of the vaccine candidates through its investments. The Tumaini trial uses a ring-vaccination approach to evaluate multiple vaccine candidates within a single study. Under this approach, researchers vaccinate contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease to assess vaccine effectiveness. The trial builds on an approach used during the West Africa Ebola outbreak a decade ago. At that time, a landmark study in Guinea established the effectiveness of Ervebo against the Zaire ebolavirus. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in the Tumaini trial to assess its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus. So far, researchers have established four vaccination rings and are preparing several more. These rings include contacts of people who have fallen ill or died from the disease. Furthermore, researchers plan to add maftivimab to the trial to assess its potential as a treatment. A separate post-exposure prophylaxis study involving obeldevisir is also underway. WHO Supports Ebola Research and Clinical Studies WHO is supporting research activities through its R&D Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme. Its efforts include developing research protocols, providing technical guidance, coordinating research partners and supporting the integration of ethical and scientifically rigorous studies into the outbreak response. Initial findings from the treatment trials are expected in the coming months, while results from the vaccine trial are anticipated in early 2027. content: 10°C overcast clouds TFL Updates Search for: Search Search LDN Write For Us Login London News Lifestyle Entrepreneurship Fitness & Health Finance Tech Food & Drink Automotive Travel Global Ebola trial advisers back two Bundibugyo vaccine candidates By LDN Editor 05 November 2026 4 minute read Listen to this article Independent advisers have recommended adding two experimental vaccines designed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus to an Ebola study under way in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The World Health Organisation said the candidates, known as ChAdOx1 and mRNA-1469, could enter the Tumaini trial after national approvals. The recommendation is not itself a regulatory approval, and neither candidate has been shown to protect people against the virus in this outbreak. ChAdOx1 is being developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India. The mRNA-1469 candidate is being developed by Moderna. An independent advisory group convened by the health organisation recommended both for further clinical evaluation after considering preclinical and early clinical evidence. The companies were informed on Monday, the organisation said in its announcement on Wednesday. It expects results from the vaccine trial in early 2027, although that is an expectation rather than a confirmed date for findings. A new stage for an existing study The recommendation follows the start of Tumaini in Bunia, in the country’s north-eastern Ituri province. The first participant was vaccinated on 23 October. The study is led by the Congolese National Institute for Biomedical Research and the University of Antwerp, with national and international partners. The two Bundibugyo-specific candidates had already been identified as possible additions to the study. The new development is the advisers’ recommendation that both be evaluated, subject to the required national approvals. It is not an announcement that vaccinations with either new candidate have already begun. Tumaini is a phase 2/3 trial designed to assess the safety, immune response and effectiveness of vaccine candidates. Its adaptive structure allows more than one candidate to be examined within the same study, rather than requiring a wholly separate trial for each one. The study uses a ring-vaccination approach, enrolling contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. The World Health Organisation said four vaccination rings were already in place and several more were being prepared. The rings include contacts of people who became ill or died from Ebola. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in the study. It is licensed against Ebola virus, also known as Zaire ebolavirus, but was not designed specifically for Bundibugyo. Researchers are assessing whether it offers protection against the virus responsible for the current outbreak; that protection has not been established. The proposed additions address a different question: whether vaccines designed for Bundibugyo can safely protect people exposed to that virus. The health organisation said their evaluation would be the first time specifically designed candidates had been tested during an outbreak of the disease. Research alongside the response Bundibugyo is one of several viruses that can cause Ebola disease. There is no licensed vaccine specifically against it. The disease can spread through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials, and early supportive care can improve a patient’s chance of survival. Finding a vaccine is only one part of the response. Health teams also work to identify infections, trace contacts, care for patients and support safe, dignified burials. Those measures continue while researchers gather evidence; the recommendation does not establish that transmission has stopped. A separate treatment study is assessing the antibody MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir and a combination of the two in patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. The health organisation said another antibody, maftivimab, would soon be added. These are investigations into treatment, not proof that the medicines work against Bundibugyo. For the vaccine candidates, the next steps are national approvals and their entry into the trial. The results will be needed to establish how well the products perform and whether they can offer a useful additional tool for future outbreak responses. Featured image: AI-generated illustration. content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Ebola Cases Top 10,000 in Congo as Africa CDC Toll Shows More Than Half of Patients Have Died By Avery Porter Published: Nov 06 2026, 7:32 AM EST Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail Tony KARUMBA | AFP via Getty Images Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Information may change as health agencies release additional findings. CDC figures are data through Nov. 1, 2026, from a page updated Nov. 3. Africa CDC death figures were reported Nov. 2, 2026, with Congo data through Oct. 31. The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has passed 10,000 confirmed cases, and Africa CDC's latest count shows more than half of infected people have died. Africa CDC reported 5,376 deaths as of Nov. 2, according to Al Jazeera, with about 10,444 infections across Congo, Uganda, and Kenya. The U.S. CDC's situation page, using confirmed cases only, lists 10,563 cases and 5,130 deaths through Nov. 1. By that measure, just under half of confirmed patients have died. Either way, the outbreak crossed two grim thresholds in the same week — and it is now among the deadliest Ebola epidemics on record. Two Agencies, Two Counts, One Trend The difference between the two tallies matters for readers trying to understand the numbers. CDC counts confirmed cases and confirmed deaths separately and excludes suspected cases pending investigation. Africa CDC's figures, given to reporters, were compiled on a different schedule. Neither agency explained the gap publicly, and the true fatality rate may shift as recent patients recover or die. What both counts show is a death rate far higher than many recent outbreaks. The World Health Organization says Ebola fatality has ranged from about 25% to 90% in past outbreaks. Euronews, citing AFP, described this as the fastest-growing and most widespread Ebola epidemic on record. Nature World News previously reported that cases were nearing 10,000 as Congo launched its first vaccine trial and the U.S. added a travel attestation. At that time, CDC data through Oct. 23 showed 9,847 cases and 4,761 deaths. In roughly nine days, about 700 more confirmed cases and nearly 370 more deaths were added. The Strain That Existing Shots Were Not Built For Bundibugyo is one of several viruses that cause Ebola disease, and it is rare. Before 2026, it had caused only two known outbreaks, in Uganda in 2007 and Congo in 2012, each with fewer than 60 cases. That rarity is the core problem — the vaccine and antibody treatments developed over the past decade target Zaire ebolavirus, the species behind the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic. The Associated Press reports none is approved for Bundibugyo. Doctors in Congo are now testing whether Ervebo, the licensed Zaire vaccine, offers any cross-protection, with Bundibugyo-specific candidates expected to follow. No result from that trial has been published. Conflict compounds the medical gap. Eastern Congo has seen attacks on Ebola facilities and displacement, which slows contact tracing and keeps sick people from early care. Early in the outbreak, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned that responders were "playing catch-up" after delayed detection. Where the Virus Has Spread CDC lists confirmed cases in eight Congolese provinces: Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Sud-Ubangi, Tshopo and Nord-Ubangi. Ituri, the original epicenter around Bunia, has carried the largest share. Beyond Congo, Uganda recorded 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over. Kenya confirmed its first-ever Ebola cases in October, nine in all with two deaths, all in Nairobi and all linked to the first patient. Kenya's health ministry has reported no community spread. Nigeria confirmed one imported case on Oct. 20 in Abuja. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said that the patient and a close contact were medically evacuated to Switzerland on Oct. 26. France treated one case in July, and that patient has recovered. Low Risk at Home, New Rules at the Airport For Americans, the official message is unchanged. "The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low," the CDC states. CDC's case table lists no cases in the United States. What has changed is airport procedure. After 11:59 p.m. EST on Nov. 3, every passenger on an international flight to the United States must attest they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. Travelers who were in Congo within 21 days cannot board commercial flights to the U.S. U.S. citizens and nationals arriving from Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. CDC's Level 4 notice tells Americans to avoid all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces. It advises reconsidering nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo, and enhanced precautions elsewhere in Congo and in Uganda. The people most affected by these rules are aid workers, health care staff, missionaries, business travelers and families with relatives in the region. Anyone with recent travel to an affected area who develops fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhea or unexplained bleeding within 21 days should call a doctor or health department before arriving at a clinic, so staff can prepare. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a sick person, not through casual contact or the air. Several important questions remain unanswered. It is not yet known whether Ervebo protects against Bundibugyo, whether the Kenya and Nigeria clusters are fully contained, or whether cases in Ituri are truly declining. The next data points to watch are CDC's weekly situation updates, WHO's Disease Outbreak News reports, and early findings from the vaccine trial. The milestone is grim, and the outbreak is not under control. Still, the danger remains concentrated in eastern Congo and among people with direct exposure. For U.S. readers, the practical step is limited to travel awareness and early reporting of symptoms after time in affected areas. CDC lists 10,532 confirmed cases in Congo and 10,563 across all affected countries, with data through Nov. 1, 2026. Is the death rate really above 50%? Africa CDC's count puts deaths slightly above half of infections. CDC's confirmed-only count is just under half. The rate may change as recent cases resolve. Why is Bundibugyo harder to fight? Approved Ebola vaccines and antibody treatments target a different species, Zaire ebolavirus. None is approved for Bundibugyo. Which countries have reported cases? Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, and France. Uganda and France have no active cases. What is the risk to Americans? CDC says the overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. content: Skip to main content Edition: ENInternational Edition Kosovo Albania International Deutsch Health Where is the British doctor with Ebola being treated? A London isolation unit, and the public risk is low A British doctor who caught Ebola in DR Congo is in the Royal Free Hospital's high-level isolation unit in London. UKHSA says the risk to the wider public remains low. By Nacionale News · November 6, 2026, 5:32 a.m. ET4 min read Photo: Matt Brown / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 The British doctor who caught Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being treated in the high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free Hospital in London, and the UK Health Security Agency says the risk to the wider public remains low, according to the Department of Health and Social Care. Ebola does not spread through the air: it passes through direct contact with the bodily fluids of someone who has symptoms. The doctor’s name, condition and how they were exposed have not been released. So yes, there is now one confirmed Ebola patient in the UK. The patient is in a sealed unit built for this purpose, and the NHS says Ebola has never been spread from person to person in the UK. What happened The doctor had been working on the Ebola epidemic in DR Congo and tested positive there. The UK and DRC governments and international health partners arranged a medical evacuation flight, and the patient arrived on Thursday 5 November, according to the government statement and the Associated Press. The government says the flight followed established infection prevention and control procedures, which also cover everyone involved in the patient’s care. The AP reports that this is the first British patient evacuated from the current outbreak and the third person with a positive test to be returned to Europe. A doctor in France who fell ill after a humanitarian mission in Congo was confirmed in June and has since recovered, the AP says. What UKHSA and the NHS say about the risk Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of UKHSA’s All Hazards Public Health Response, said the risk to the wider public “remains low”, in the government statement. She told the AP that “robust infection prevention and control protocols are in place”. According to the government, the Royal Free unit has strict protocols so the patient has no contact with members of the public, and staff wear protective equipment and follow other measures to stop transmission. The NHS Ebola page also describes the risk to people in the UK as low. Inside the Royal Free isolation unit The Royal Free in Hampstead, north London, has a high-level isolation unit run by a dedicated team of doctors, nurses and laboratory staff. It has treated patients with Lassa fever, Ebola and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever before, LBC reports. Access is restricted, staff care for the patient through a special tent with controlled ventilation, and all air leaving the unit is cleaned, according to LBC. The unit also treated patients during the 2014 to 2015 West Africa outbreak, the AP notes. In March 2015, for example, a UK military healthcare worker diagnosed in Sierra Leone was flown to the Royal Free, according to a government release from the time. Before this case, only four confirmed Ebola cases had been recorded in the UK: one in 1976 after a needle incident in a laboratory, and three health workers during the West Africa outbreak, LBC reports. How Ebola spreads, and how it does not It spreads through contact with the body fluids of an infected person or wild animal, such as blood, vomit, saliva and urine (NHS). It does not spread through the air (DHSC and UKHSA). People are generally not infectious until they develop symptoms, Dr Damien Tully of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine told LBC. Symptoms can appear 2 to 21 days after infection. They often start suddenly, like flu, with fever, extreme tiredness and headache, and can later include vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and bleeding or bruising (NHS). Tully called the infection “deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected”, according to the AP, because health workers can be exposed by accident even with careful protection. He told LBC the case does not suggest the virus has become more transmissible. The outbreak in DR Congo The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, one of the Ebola viruses. As of 4 November, DR Congo had reported 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 related deaths across eight provinces, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. The AP says it has spread to 67 health zones, from three when it was declared in May. Other patients from the outbreak have been evacuated to Switzerland and the Netherlands, the ECDC reports. What to do if you are worried The NHS says to call NHS 111 if you have travelled to an affected country and have symptoms, or have been in contact with a traveller who has symptoms. Stay at home and avoid close contact with others until you are told what to do. Contact with the general public is not a concern in this case: the patient travelled on a medical evacuation flight and went straight into isolation, according to the government. What we don’t know The doctor’s name, age and current condition have not been released. How and when the doctor was exposed in DR Congo has not been made public. Officials have not said what treatment the doctor is receiving. No official statement has said whether anyone else who worked with the doctor is being monitored. Read more Is Ebola in the UK? Tropical Medicine London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine https://lshtm.ac.uk/themes/custom/lshtm/images/lshtm-logo-black.png Share LSHTM expert says the risk from planned medical evacuation is low and incident does not suggest UK public is at increased risk Illustration of Ebola virus showing long thin curving light blue filament with two loops and wing-like structure on lefthand side and righthand end curving upwards against dark blue background The UK government has confirmed that a British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has been flown back to the UK in a planned medical evacuation. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola linked to the ongoing outbreak centred on DRC caused by Bundibugyo virus. So far the outbreak has led to over 5,000 deaths. The man, who is a medical doctor, was infected while working for a humanitarian organisation as part of the response to the outbreak. He was transported to the Royal Free Hospital, London, on 5 November 2026. Dr Damien Tully, Associate Professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (MRC/UVRI and LSHTM) Uganda Research Unit said: “The infection of a British healthcare worker with Ebola is deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected. Healthcare workers are on the frontline of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur. "This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased. “Unlike respiratory viruses such as COVID-19 and influenza, that can spread through the air, Ebola is transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms. This means that identifying and isolating cases, together with appropriate infection prevention measures, can be highly effective in preventing onward transmission. For the UK public, the risk from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low. “The UK has well-established procedures for managing cases of viral haemorrhagic fever, including two dedicated high-level isolation units at the Royal Free Hospital in London and the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. These facilities are equipped with specialist isolation systems and staffed by highly trained infectious disease teams. Patients can be transported under carefully controlled conditions, with strict infection prevention measures, appropriate protective equipment and arrangements for identifying and monitoring anyone who may have been exposed. “Crucially, a planned medical evacuation such as this allows established protocols within the NHS England specialist infectious disease network to be activated in advance, ensuring that healthcare teams, transport arrangements and isolation facilities are coordinated before the patient arrives. These measures substantially reduce the risk of onward transmission to healthcare workers and the wider public. “The UK has been here before. During the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic, three infected healthcare workers were treated in the UK, including two who were medically evacuated from Sierra Leone. All three recovered, with no onward transmission in the UK. This experience provides reassurance that specialist isolation facilities and established infection prevention procedures can successfully manage patients infected overseas while minimising the risk of onward transmission. "While this case is understandably attracting attention in the UK, the greatest danger remains in the communities affected by the outbreak in the DRC and elsewhere in the region. Protecting frontline healthcare workers, rapidly identifying and isolating cases, and interrupting transmission at its source remain critical to preventing further infections and international spread.” This is a rapid reaction to a breaking news story. This story was updated on 5 November 2026 to reflect that the man had been transported to the Royal Free Hospital, London and on 6 November 2026 to confirm the man is a medical doctor. content: Latest News Syria Middle East Economy Politics Sport International Reading: WHO recommends two new vaccine candidates for Ebola trials AR TR FR ES KU Latest News Syria Middle East Economy Politics Sport International Reading: WHO recommends two new vaccine candidates for Ebola trials AR TR FR ES KU Culture Video Photos Miscellaneous Latest News Syria Middle East Economy Politics Sport International Search Latest News News Categories Politics Culture Video Photos Miscellaneous Provinces Languages العربية Türkçe Français Español Kurdî Follow US WHO recommends two new vaccine candidates for Ebola trials Published: 2026/11/05 10:57 AM Updated: 2026/11/05 10:59 AM World Health Organization (WHO) Logo – Geneva Geneva, Nov. 5 (SANA) The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended adding two experimental vaccine candidates to clinical trials targeting the Bundibugyo virus, amid the ongoing outbreak in Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where the death toll has exceeded 5,300. In a statement published on its website on Wednesday, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization’s expert groups had recommended including the two candidates in trials that began last month using the Ervebo vaccine. Ervebo is approved for protection against Ebola virus disease but is not approved for the Bundibugyo virus currently spreading in the DRC. The two candidates are ChAdOx1 BDBV, developed by the University of Oxford in cooperation with India’s Serum Institute, and mRNA-1469, developed by Moderna. Both are designed to target the Bundibugyo virus, Ghebreyesus said. On Nov. 2, Ghebreyesus said the outbreak in the DRC underscored the urgent need to finalize the international agreement on pandemics and strengthen cooperation among countries to address health threats that cross borders.
